description: I'm looking for motivated, creative teammates who enjoy sharing ideas and learning together. I'd especially love to work with people interested in web development, UI/UX design, data analysis, or scientific research. Let's build something meaningful together!
summary:
MARS Mission is a browser-based game we built where players, ages 7–12, become junior astronauts on a Mars base. With their robot buddy ROVA, they explore the habitat, fix critical machines, and learn that survival on Mars is a chain of connected systems: dust on solar panels cuts power, low power slows the water recycler and greenhouse, and every lost crew member costs precious crew-hours.
We developed this for the NASA Space Apps "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge. Mission 1 is a short, guided story—a dust storm knocks out the lights, and the player wipes the panels clean to bring the base back to life. Free Play is the deeper trainer: over 30 sols, players face five competing repairs they can't all afford, read a weather forecast, and make hard choices about where to spend limited time and energy. Every outcome is explained in plain language, so kids learn why systems fail, not just what button to press.
We based the Mars conditions on real data modeled from Curiosity and Perseverance, turning planetary science into a hands-on lesson in resourcefulness—and it runs on any phone or laptop, no install required.
details:
Mars Mission is a browser game for kids ages 7–12 where you play as a junior astronaut managing a Mars base alongside ROVA, a friendly robot guide. Instead of shooting aliens or racing a clock, your job is to keep a small crew alive by making smart decisions with limited resources.

In Mission 1, a dust storm buries the solar panels and kills the power, so you have to physically wipe them clean in a minigame to bring the lights back. Free Play is a 30-sol survival challenge where five critical repairs compete for your time and battery—and you can't afford to fix them all. You read the weather forecast, weigh trade-offs, and live with the consequences. A recap screen explains what happened in plain language, so kids learn systems thinking and resilience through play, not lectures.

The goal is to spark genuine curiosity about STEM by making abstract Mars science—like dust opacity and power budgets—tangible. It’s designed to be the kind of game a kid plays once and then asks, "Wait, how do real solar panels work on Mars?"

We built the game using HTML5, JavaScript, and the Phaser 3 engine. To speed up development, we used AI to help write the game logic, simulation code, and draw the procedural art. We tested it with Python Playwright and a Node.js bot simulator to check balance across thousands of runs. The Mars conditions are based on real data from NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers.

The creative heart of the project is the interlocking simulation—everything feeds into everything else, teaching cause and effect. We made sure it works on phones, tablets, and laptops with touch, mouse, and keyboard controls, and we included a gentler "Friendly crew" mode for younger players. We were also honest with our science communication, clearly labeling the game as "inspired by NASA data" rather than raw mission data.
